nameStory: The 'tenlobe' in this plant's name refers to the ten distinctive lobes or segments found on each flower's corolla - more than most of its false foxglove relatives. It's called a 'false' foxglove because while its tubular pink flowers look similar to true foxgloves, it belongs to an entirely different plant family and lacks the heart medication compounds that make true foxgloves famous.
description: Tenlobe false foxglove is a slender annual wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with a delicate, branching appearance. Its most striking feature is its pink to purple tubular flowers that bloom along thin, wiry stems from late summer into fall. The plant has a somewhat scraggly growth habit with narrow, deeply-lobed leaves that give it an airy, fine-textured look. Unlike many wildflowers, this species is actually parasitic, stealing nutrients from the roots of grasses and other plants around it.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pink to purple tubular flowers with ten distinct lobes around the opening, creating a frilly, ruffled appearance that feels papery to the touch when mature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow leaves deeply divided into thread-like segments, giving them a feathery texture that feels almost needle-like when rubbed between fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, branching stems that feel somewhat brittle and create an open, delicate framework usually 1-3 feet tall

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small round capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny seeds that rattle inside when the dried capsule is shaken

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, wiry stems that are often reddish-tinged and feel smooth but somewhat rigid, branching frequently in the upper portions

habitat: Look for tenlobe false foxglove in sandy or rocky open areas, particularly coastal plains, pine barrens, and dry grasslands throughout New England. It favors well-drained, acidic soils and is often found growing among grasses, sedges, and low shrubs in sunny locations. This species seems to prefer areas with some disturbance, like edges of trails, old fields, or clearings where it can parasitize the roots of nearby grasses.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with finely-divided leaves, but are easily overlooked among other vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow taller and begin branching, with flower buds forming in late summer but not yet open.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming period from August through October, when the distinctive pink flowers with ten lobes are most visible and diagnostic.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with dried seed capsules still attached, appearing as delicate brown skeletons.

funFact: This sneaky plant is actually a 'green vampire' - while it can photosynthesize like other plants, it secretly taps into the root systems of nearby grasses to steal water and nutrients, making it what botanists call a hemiparasite.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other false foxgloves, but the ten-lobed flowers are distinctive - purple false foxglove has only five lobes, and slender false foxglove has much smaller flowers with less obvious lobing. Memory trick: 'Ten-lobe' literally tells you what to count!
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'false foxglove,' this plant is completely unrelated to true foxgloves (Digitalis) and lacks their medicinal properties. The false foxgloves were moved from the snapdragon family to the broomrape family relatively recently as scientists better understood their parasitic lifestyle.
compareHints: Tenlobe false foxglove is distinguished from other New England false foxgloves primarily by its flower structure - it has ten corolla lobes versus five in most relatives, and tends to have more deeply divided, thread-like leaves than purple false foxglove. It's also typically found in sandier, more coastal habitats compared to the grassland preferences of slender false foxglove.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple false foxglove is the most common and robust of the false foxgloves in New England, with larger flowers and broader leaves than slender false foxglove.
Among New England's false foxgloves, slender false foxglove has the thinnest, most thread-like leaves - much narrower than purple false foxglove's broader lance-shaped leaves.
Saltmarsh false foxglove is the only member of its genus that requires salty conditions - this habitat preference makes it the easiest false foxglove to identify.
Compared to its false foxglove relatives, Nova Scotia false foxglove is distinguished mainly by its coastal habitat requirement and very limited range.
Beach false foxglove differs from its relatives like purple false foxglove and slender false foxglove primarily by its coastal habitat and extremely narrow, thread-like leaves.
